4194               	; 	' ======================================================================
4195               	; 	' TITLE
4196               	; 	' ======================================================================
4197               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
4198               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
4199               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
4200               	; 	' until everything was ready.
4201               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
4202               	; 	'
4203               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
4204               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
4205               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
4206               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
4207               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
4208               	; 	'
4209               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
4210               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
4211               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
4212               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
4213               	; 	'
4214               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
4215               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
4216               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
4217               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
4218               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.

4225               	; 	' entry 0 is the same colour, so it cannot be set per region the way the
4226               	; 	' sky and the store are. It was never written at all, which is why every
4227               	; 	' cell that maps to index 0 came out black, the title page included.
4228               	; 	'
4229               	; 	' Writing it here and putting it back in draw_screen costs two statements
4230               	; 	' and no art: the title is almost entirely index 0, so the backdrop IS its
4231               	; 	' background. The store wants black back -- its outlines, the HUD row and
4232               	; 	' the space under the scanner all read as index 0 -- so draw_screen resets
4233               	; 	' it rather than leaving the store tinted.

4410               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
4411               	; 	'
4412               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
4413               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
4414               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
4415               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
4416               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
4417               	; 	'
4418               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
4419               	; 	'
4420               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
4421               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
4422               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
4423               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
4424               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
4425               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
4426               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
4427               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
4428               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
4429               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
4430               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
4431               	; 	'
4432               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
4433               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
4434               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
4435               	; 	'
4436               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
4437               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
4438               	;

4483               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
4484               	; 	'
4485               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
4486               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
4487               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
4488               	; 	' picture.
4489               	; 	'
4490               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
4491               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
4492               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
4493               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
4494               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
4495               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
4496               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
4497               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
4498               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
4499               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
4500               	; 	' same picture.
4501               	; 	'
4502               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
4503               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
4504               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
4505               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
4506               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
4507               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1

4528               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for

4572               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
4573               	; 		'
4574               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
4575               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
4576               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
4577               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
4578               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
4579               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.

4582               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4583               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4584               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
4585               	; 		'
4586               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4587               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4588               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4589               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4590               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.

4720               	;
4721               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4722               	; 	'
4723               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4724               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4725               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4726               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4727               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4728               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4729               	; 	'
4730               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4731               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4732               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4733               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4734               	; 	'

4736               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.

5459               	;
5460               	; 	' ======================================================================
5461               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5462               	; 	' ======================================================================
5463               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5464               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5465               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5466               	; 	' of running.
5467               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5468               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5469               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5470               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5471               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5472               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5473               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5474               	; 	'
5475               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5476               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5477               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5478               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5479               	; 	'
5480               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5481               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5482               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5483               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5484               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5485               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5486               	; 	'
5487               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5488               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5489               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5490               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5491               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5492               	; 	'
5493               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5494               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5495               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5496               	; draw_screen:
5497               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5569               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5570               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5571               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5572               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5573               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5574               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5575               	; 		'
5576               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5577               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5578               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5579               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5580               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5581               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5582               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5583               	; 		'
5584               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5585               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.

5587               	; 		WAIT

5643               	;
5644               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5645               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5646               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5647               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5648               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5649               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5650               	; 	'
5651               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5652               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5653               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5654               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5655               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5656               	; 	'
5657               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5658               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5659               	; 	' above it at all.
5660               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5661               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5662               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5663               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5664               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's

6306               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between

6315               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64

6317               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At

6435               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6436               	; 			'
6437               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6438               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6439               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6440               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6441               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6442               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6443               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6444               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6445               	; 			'
6446               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6447               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6448               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6449               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6450               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6451               	; 			'
6452               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6453               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6454               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6455               	; 			'
6456               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6457               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6458               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6459               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6460               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6461               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.

6463               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every

7387               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7388               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7389               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7390               	; 		'
7391               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7392               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7393               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7394               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7395               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
7396               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
7397               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7398               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7399               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
7400               	; 		'
7401               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on
7402               	; 		' the floor and the bottom tread is 4 to 7 px above them, so he
7403               	; 		' climbs at 2 px a pass until he catches it (the tread is rising at
7404               	; 		' 1, so the gap closes at 1 a pass) and then rides with it. Jumping
7405               	; 		' on he lands ON a tread, so eson is 0 and this never runs.

8398               	;
8399               	; 	' HE STANDS ON THE STAIRS, IN A SLOT HE BORROWS.
8400               	; 	'
8401               	; 	' hsw is which art is resident: 0 running, 1 standing-right, 2
8402               	; 	' standing-left. Both routines return immediately when nothing has to
8403               	; 	' change, so a ride costs one set of copies rather than one per pass.
8404               	; 	'
8405               	; 	' THE FACING COMES FROM THE FLIGHT, NOT FROM hdir. Riding UP he travels
8406               	; 	' towards the flight's head -- west for a west flight -- and riding DOWN
8407               	; 	' he travels the other way along the same staircase, so the direction is
8408               	; 	' the pair (hst, hesd) and not either one alone. hdir is set from it here
8409               	; 	' so the FACE, which is not borrowed, agrees with the body.
8410               	; 	'
8411               	; 	' Nested IFs rather than `hst = 1 AND hesd = 1`: CVBasic's 9900 backend
8412               	; 	' miscompiles a compound comparison (CLAUDE.md 3A).

8864               	;
8865               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8866               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8867               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8868               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8869               	; 	'
8870               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8871               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8872               	; 	'
8873               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8874               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8875               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8876               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8877               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8878               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8879               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8880               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8881               	; 	' merged object.
8882               	; 	'
8883               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8884               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8885               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8886               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8887               	; 	'
8888               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8889               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8890               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8891               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8892               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8893               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8894               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8895               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8896               	; 	'
8897               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8898               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8899               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8900               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8901               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8902               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8903               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8904               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8905               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8906               	; 	'
8907               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8908               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8909               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8910               	; 	#if NES
8911               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8912               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8913               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8914               	; 	'
8915               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8916               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8917               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8918               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8919               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8920               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8921               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8922               	; 	'
8923               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8924               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8925               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8926               	; 	'
8927               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8928               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8929               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8930               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8931               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8932               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8933               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8934               	; 	'
8935               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8936               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8937               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8938               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8939               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8940               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8941               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8942               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8943               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8944               	; 	'
8945               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8946               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8947               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8948               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8949               	; 	'
8950               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8951               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8952               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8953               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8954               	; nes_swp16:
8955               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8956               	; 	'
8957               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8958               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8959               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8960               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8961               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8962               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8963               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8964               	; 	'
8965               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8966               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8967               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8968               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8969               	; 	'
8970               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8971               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8972               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8973               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8974               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8975               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8976               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8977               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0

9001               	; nes_def:
9002               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9003               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9004               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9005               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9006               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9007               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9008               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9009               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9010               	; 	RETURN
9011               	;
9012               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9013               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9014               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9015               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9016               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9017               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9018               	; 	'

9022               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9023               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9024               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9025               	; 	'
9026               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9027               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9028               	; nes_escd:

9125               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps
9126               	; 	' both into the slab row of the band above, but they mean different
9127               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9128               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9129               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9130               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9131               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9132               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9133               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9134               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9135               	; 	' nothing.
9136               	; 	'
9137               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9138               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9139               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9140               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9141               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to
9142               	; 	' reach column 0 or 31.
9143               	; beam_clear:
9144               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9145               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9146               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9147               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9148               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9149               	; 	'
9150               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9151               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --
9152               	; 	' and clearing structure because an erase routine could not tell the
9153               	; 	' two apart is the fault that once deleted the second floor's support.

9831               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
9832               	; 	'
9833               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
9834               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9835               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9836               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9837               	; 	'
9838               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9839               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9840               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9841               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9842               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9843               	; 	' clear it.
9844               	; 	pacc = obac

10089               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10090               	; 	'
10091               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10092               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10093               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10094               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10095               	; 	'
10096               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10097               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10098               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10099               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10100               	; 	'
10101               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10102               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10103               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10104               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10105               	; 	'
10106               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10107               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10108               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10109               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10110               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10111               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10599               	;
10600               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10601               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10602               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10603               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10604               	; 	' runs every pass.
10605               	; 	'
10606               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10607               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10608               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10609               	; 	'
10610               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10611               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10612               	; 	'
10613               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10614               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10615               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10616               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10617               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10618               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10619               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10620               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10621               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10622               	; 	'
10623               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10624               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10625               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10626               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10627               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10628               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10629               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10630               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10631               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10632               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10633               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10634               	; 	' flight looking busy.
10635               	; 	'
10636               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.
10637               	; 	'
10638               	; 	' THE KOP ARRIVING ON THIS FLOOR OUTRANKS IT. This used to override the
10639               	; 	' flee as well as the climb, so for the whole of the run he held one
10640               	; 	' heading no matter where Kelly was -- and ran straight into him without
10641               	; 	' appearing to notice he was there. The flee above has already worked out
10642               	; 	' which way is away; clearing the run simply lets it stand.
10643               	; 	'
10644               	; 	' AND REACHING THE END WALL ENDS IT. It used to be a count of passes,
10645               	; 	' which expired somewhere in the middle of a floor and turned him round

10731               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10732               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10733               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10734               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10735               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10736               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10737               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10738               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10739               	; 	'
10740               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10741               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10742               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10743               	; 	'
10744               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10745               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10746               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10747               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10748               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10749               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10750               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10751               	; 	'
10752               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10753               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10754               	; 	'
10755               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10756               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10757               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10758               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10759               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10760               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10761               	; 	'
10762               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10763               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10764               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10765               	; 	' before any of this.
10766               	; 	'
10767               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10768               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10769               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10770               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10771               	; 	' journey.
10772               	; 	'
10773               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10774               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10775               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11236               	;
11237               	; 	' ======================================================================
11238               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11239               	; 	' ======================================================================
11240               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11241               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11242               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11243               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11244               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11245               	; 	'
11246               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11247               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11248               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11249               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11250               	; 	' broken.
11251               	; 	'
11252               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11253               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11254               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11255               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11256               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11257               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11258               	; 	'
11259               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11260               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11261               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11262               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11263               	; coll_obst:
11264               cvb_COLL_OBST

11630               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11631               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11632               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11633               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11634               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11635               	; 	' away from.
11636               	; 	'
11637               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11638               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11639               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11640               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11641               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11642               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11643               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11644               	; 	'
11645               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11646               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11647               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11648               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11649               	; 	'
11650               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
11651               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.

11654               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once

11823               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as

11826               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".

11828               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11829               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11830               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.

13018               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13019               	; 	' ======================================================================
13020               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13021               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13022               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13023               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13024               	; 	'
13025               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13026               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13027               	; 	'
13028               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13029               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13030               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13031               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13032               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13033               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13034               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13035               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13036               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13037               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13038               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
13039               	; esc_tick:

13064               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13065               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13066               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13067               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13068               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13069               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13070               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13071               	; 	'

13073               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13074               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13075               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13076               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13077               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13078               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13092               	; 	#if NES
13093               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13094               	; 	'
13095               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13096               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13097               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13098               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13099               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13100               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13101               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13102               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13103               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13104               	; 	'
13105               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13106               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13107               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13108               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13109               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13110               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13111               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13112               	; 	'
13113               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13114               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13115               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13116               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13117               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13118               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13119               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13120               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13121               	; 	' with room to spare.
13122               	; 	'
13123               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13124               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13125               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13126               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13127               	; 	WAIT
13128               	; 	#endif
13129               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13130               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13131               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13132               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13133               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13134               	; 	'
13135               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13136               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13137               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13138               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13139               	; 	'
13140               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13141               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13142               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13143               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13144               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13145               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13146               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13147               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13148               	; 	'
13149               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13150               	; 	' move at all.

13477               	;
13478               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13479               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13480               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13481               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13482               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13483               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13484               	; 	'
13485               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13486               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13487               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13488               	; 	'
13489               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13490               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13491               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13492               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13493               	; 	'
13494               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13495               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13496               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13497               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13498               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13499               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13500               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13501               	; 	'
13502               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13503               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13504               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
13505               	; 	'
13506               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
13507               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why
13508               	; 	' scan_escs and scan_elev redraw every tick rather than once.

13780               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13781               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
13782               	; 	'

13784               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13785               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13786               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,

13942               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out

13944               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13945               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13946               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single

13951               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13952               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13953               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13954               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13955               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13956               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13957               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13958               	; 	'
13959               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13960               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13961               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13962               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13963               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13964               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13965               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13966               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13967               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13968               	; 	'
13969               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13970               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13971               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13972               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13973               	; 	'
13974               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13975               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.

13979               	; 	#if NES
13980               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
13981               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
13982               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a

13999               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
14000               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
14001               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
14002               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
14003               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
14004               	; 	'
14005               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
14006               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
14007               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
14008               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
14009               	; 	'
14010               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
14011               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
14012               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
14013               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
14014               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
14015               	; 	'
14016               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
14017               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
14018               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
14019               	; 	'
14020               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
14021               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).
14022               	; 	' The outer eight are deliberate air, four above and four below, so the
14023               	; 	' radar does not butt against the shop floor above it or the screen edge
14024               	; 	' below. On the TI those rows take the scanner's own background; here they
14025               	; 	' are index 2, the store's grey, against the instrument's green.
14026               	; 	'
14027               	; 	' Two bitplanes give the four colours this canvas needs and nothing else
14028               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
14029               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
14030               	; 	'
14031               	; 	' The byte's place in the canvas says which it is. 256 bytes is one
14032               	; 	' CHARACTER row (16 tiles of 16), the low three bits are the pixel row
14033               	; 	' within the tile, and bit 3 of the position picks the bitplane.
14034               	; 	FOR swj = 0 TO 11

14039               	; 			' NO MARGIN INSIDE THE CANVAS. All twenty-four pixel

14645               	;
14646               	; #if NES
14647               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14648               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14649               	; 	' screen different colours.
14650               	; 	'
14651               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14652               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14653               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14654               	; 	'
14655               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14656               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14657               	; 	'
14658               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14659               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14660               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14661               	; 	'
14662               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14663               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14664               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14665               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14666               	; 	'
14667               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14668               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14669               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14670               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES WHITE ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14671               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14672               	; 	'
14673               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14674               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14675               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14676               	; 	' palette, dark blue and white, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14677               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14678               	; 	'
14679               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14680               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14681               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14682               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14683               	; 	'
14684               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14685               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14686               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14687               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14688               	; 	' these beside it.
14689               	; 	'
14690               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14691               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14692               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14693               	; nes_boxatt:
14694               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 3
14695               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
14696               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14697               	; 	NEXT nai
14698               	; 	RETURN
14699               	;
14700               	; nes_attr:
14701               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
14702               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
14703               	; 	'
14704               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
14705               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
14706               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
14707               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
14708               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
14709               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band
14710               	; 	' of dark blue running into the sky.
14711               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14712               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
14713               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14714               	; 	NEXT nai
14715               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14716               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170			' $AA -- the whole sky band on P2, no second palette
14717               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14718               	; 	NEXT nai
14719               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 47
14720               	; 		VPOKE #nav,0
14721               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1

15185               	;
15186               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15187               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15188               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15189               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15190               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15191               	; 	'
15192               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15193               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15194               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15195               	; 	'
15196               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15197               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15198               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15199               	; 	'
15200               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15201               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15202               	; 	'
15203               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15204               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15205               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15206               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15207               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15208               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15209               	; 	'
15210               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15211               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15212               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15213               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15214               	; 	'
15215               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15216               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15217               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15218               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

15335               	;
15336               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15337               	; 	'
15338               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15339               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15340               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15341               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15342               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15343               	; 	'
15344               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15345               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15346               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15347               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15348               	; 	' counting stops.
15349               	;
15350               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15351               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15352               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15353               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15354               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15355               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15356               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15357               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15358               	; 	'
15359               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15360               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15361               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15405 EFFC EE42     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15406               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
15407               	; 	'
15408               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15409               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15410               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15411               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15412               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15413               	; 	'
15414               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15415               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15416               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15417               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15418               	; 	'
15419               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15420               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15421               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15422               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15423               	; 	'
15424               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15425               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15426               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15427               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15428               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15429               	; 	'
15430               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
15431               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
15432               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
15433               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
15434               	; 	'
15435               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
15436               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the
15437               	; 	' last one draws two more ON TOP, so GAME OVER appears above the reason
15438               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
15439               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
